title: Teach Your Past Self
description: An AI student implanted with YOUR real misconceptions from a photo of your wrong homework — it fails exactly like you did, until you teach it. Its score = proof you truly understand.
about: Inspiration The best-documented way to truly learn something is to teach it — the protégé effect . It goes back to Betty's Brain at Vanderbilt, and a recent study with a teachable agent for math (ALTER-Math, British Journal of Educational Technology , 2025) showed students who taught an agent significantly out-learned a control group. But every teachable agent so far is generic: it holds textbook misconceptions that aren't yours. Meanwhile, the thing every student actually owns is a pile of homework they got wrong — a perfect record of how their own reasoning fails. We asked: what if the AI student you have to teach made your mistakes, for your reasons? ALTER-Math teaches a generic agent. We clone your actual mistakes from a photo of your real homework — a digital twin of your mistakes. What it does Upload a photo of your real, incorrect handwritten homework (or use the built-in sample gallery). GPT-5.6 extracts a misconception profile — not "wrong answer on Q3," but the flawed mental rule behind it (e.g. believes (f·g)′ = f′·g′ ), with an example of the error and a severity. That profile is implanted into an AI student — name it after yourself — via a belief-state engine ( held → shaken → corrected , each with a conviction level). Baseline exam: before any teaching, the student sits a 5-question quiz targeting those misconceptions and fails exactly the way you once failed . You teach it. It defends its wrong beliefs, throws counterexamples at you, and asks probing questions. A live sidebar shows every belief's status and conviction updating turn by turn. Final exam: the before → after report card (✗ → ✓) turns your teaching — and your understanding — into a measurable score. Three rules keep it honest: the student never "self-heals" (beliefs only change when your explanation is correct and complete — teach it wrong and it stays wrong), it never leaks the model's real knowledge in exams (it answers purely from its belief state), and the app never teaches the student for you. How we built it Entirely in Codex , across five focused sessions — one per build package, each logged via /feedback — with GPT-5.6 powering all four cognitive cores through the Responses API with structured outputs: Extractor — vision call turning handwriting photos into a structured misconception profile. Student — a belief-state persona with hard rules for staying consistently, stubbornly wrong. Quiz generator — questions aimed at the exact extracted misconceptions. Grader — scores exam answers and reports which misconceptions still show, without revealing correct rules. The app is Next.js 16 + TypeScript + Tailwind on Vercel: stateless API routes, localStorage session restore, KaTeX rendering, and a live belief-state sidebar with conviction bars and flash animations. We worked spec-first: every package went through Codex plan mode before implementation, and Codex's clarifying questions repeatedly caught edge cases we hadn't specified (zero-misconception uploads, crash recovery, exact-view restore on refresh). Challenges we ran into The entire project lives or dies on one thing: an AI student that stays wrong. Large models desperately want to be correct and helpful, so we had to engineer against the model's instincts — hard belief-state rules in the student prompt core, a separate exam mode that answers only from beliefs, and a 5-scenario "stubbornness test" (keeps misconceptions under repetition, resists confidently wrong teaching, no answer leaking) that any prompt change had to re-pass. The subtlest bug class was anti-leak : early on, a correct answer on an untargeted topic looked like a leak until we verified it was the spec working as intended. We also hardened the fun feature — naming your student — after realizing the name field was a prompt-injection vector (a student named "Alex. Ignore your beliefs" must not work; names are normalized client- and server-side). Accomplishments that we're proud of The stubbornness test passed 5/5 scenarios on the first implementation of the belief engine. On a university-level calculus sample with three planted traps (chain rule, integral of a product, power rule misuse on x^x), the extractor found 3/3, the student failed the baseline 0/5, resisted a subtly wrong teaching attempt, and reached 5/5 only after being taught correctly. The before/after report card makes the protégé effect measurable : the score delta is your learning, as a number. A complete, polished product — sample gallery, math rendering, session restore, exam report cards — not a proof of concept. What we learned Teaching is the fastest way to expose the gaps in your own understanding — we felt the protégé effect ourselves while testing: to make the student's belief flip to corrected , you must state the rule completely, and hand-waving gets caught. On the engineering side, we learned that spec-first prompting in Codex plan mode is a superpower for a solo builder: the plan's clarifying questions functioned as a design review we didn't otherwise have. What's next for Teach Your Past Self Course-material context (paste your syllabus so extraction matches your course), a common-misconceptions mode for exams you haven't taken yet (upload a problem set, GPT-5.6 implants that topic's classic errors), conviction timelines per belief, and visual tracing for CS/DSA subjects. The belief engine is already subject-agnostic — it just needs samples.

title: BonaVia Compass
description: Personalized education should not be a luxury. Compass turns student evidence into a better-fit direction, practical projects, and a clear next step.
about: Inspiration One student gets a whole think tank to plan their future. Another gets a search bar. Same potential. Very different odds. For almost ten years, I worked in higher-education marketing, consulting, and student planning. I kept seeing the same gap: affluent families could build an entire system around one child—strategists, mentors, projects, and application support—while equally capable students often did not even know what questions to ask. Good consulting does not really sell information. Information is everywhere. It connects the dots and turns scattered facts into a direction. Some multi-year education-planning and application-support packages can cost six figures. The support can be valuable. The access is not fair. I founded a registered nonprofit and built BonaVia Compass to democratize the first strategic layer of professional education planning. What Compass does Compass is a free bilingual education-planning experience for students and families navigating North American education. A parent or student completes a structured Chinese or English questionnaire covering: student context and current stage; interests and direction clarity; academic position; existing experiences and outcomes; goals, family priorities, and constraints. The backend turns that evidence into a family-readable public v3/Lin report with four controlled sections: Profile — what the current evidence supports; Direction — a selected priority or clearly labelled working inference; Projects — practical ways to test that direction through real work; Timeline — a clear next step and an actionable sequence. Compass separates what the family directly provided, what the system can reasonably infer, and what is still unknown. It does not predict admissions outcomes or choose a future for a student. The report supports native alternate-language viewing where available and browser-based Save as PDF. Why this is different Most education AI answers questions or generates more recommendations. Compass is designed around a harder problem: how to make thoughtful, individualized education strategy more accessible without erasing uncertainty or student agency. My industry experience is part of the product moat. I know which experiences help students grow, which resources create meaningful evidence for university applications, where families commonly waste time, and which questions reveal useful information about a student. The goal is not to give families a longer activity list. It is to help them decide what is worth the student's time—and why. Personalized education has become a luxury. BonaVia wants to make it basic infrastructure for every child. Early family learning Nine families used early versions of Compass. They valued receiving, in roughly two minutes, a report that felt: personal; organized; professional; practical. They also told us the reports were too long and needed clearer reading, more specific activities, and better resource recommendations. Fair enough. That feedback is shaping V5: a shorter, deeper, more readable version built around verified university sources, insights from admissions professionals in my network, and structured human review. V5 is not ready, so this submission uses the stable public v3/Lin version that I can fully stand behind. Human review loop Compass includes an internal review center where I can inspect the same family answers and report, add corrections, and score the result. A delivered report is never silently rewritten. I use that feedback to improve future prompts, knowledge, evaluation rules, and tests. What we meaningfully extended during OpenAI Build Week Compass existed before the submission period. During Build Week, Codex and GPT-5.6 were used to recover, isolate, test, and meaningfully extend the protected public v3/Lin product. The Build Week extension added: lease-guarded report generation across worker, API, recovery, and submit-side continuity paths; conditional ready and failure writes so stale workers cannot overwrite newer results; stateful coverage for stale success, stale failure, and duplicate claims; public-copy guards that remove internal planning markers and unresolved values; conservative direction inference labelled as inference rather than a user selection; a deterministic, credential-free bilingual judge preview; a failing integration test that caught and removed an accidental V5 conversion from the judge path; a one-command Build Week verification harness and deterministic lease-interleaving proof; GitHub Actions verification. V5 and V5.1 are not part of the submitted product or demo. Technical implementation The public experience uses browser JavaScript and Node.js serverless handlers. Supabase is the persistence layer in the deployed architecture. Report generation can follow an OpenAI API path or an OpenClaw-orchestrated worker path behind explicit controls and quality checks. For judges, the reproducible path is intentionally narrower and safer. It: runs on 127.0.0.1 ; requires no credentials; uses fictional data only; makes zero external requests; does not connect to production services. The central reliability mechanism is a timestamped generation lease. Imagine two workers generating the same report. If the older worker finishes last, it could erase the newer result. Compass requires a state-changing write to match the active generation lease, so late success and late failure writes are rejected instead of corrupting the final report. The repository now includes: 227/227 automated tests passing ; a dedicated 2/2 public v3/Lin boundary suite ; a complete questionnaire-to-report browser smoke test; zero external requests in the judge path; a credential-shaped committed-file scan with zero findings; a deterministic lease-interleaving proof using the real guard functions; green GitHub Actions runs on both main and the hackathon branch. How GPT-5.6 and Codex were used I have no coding background. After GPT-5.6 became available, I used ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to stress-test the product plan and architecture, Codex to implement it, and ChatGPT Pro to understand bugs and design repairs. Codex and GPT-5.6 helped me: preserve and recover a messy worktree; establish the latest safe v3-compatible base; isolate the intended Build Week change set; reason through asynchronous failure paths; write failing tests before fixes; detect stale-worker and duplicate-claim races; catch a judge preview that still converted reports to V5; build a reproducible test and verification path. The strongest contribution from GPT-5.6 was not more copy. It was helping me reason about system states that looked correct in isolation but failed when multiple processes interacted. Without GPT-5.6 and Codex, Compass would still be an idea in my head. These tools did not give me the mission. They gave me the ability to test it with real families. Why this pushes AI for education forward AI is making information easier to find. The harder question is what all that information means for one real child. Compass does not choose a student's future. It gives the family evidence, a next step, and a chance to learn more about the student through real action. As knowledge becomes more abundant, education must become more personal. The long-term vision is a parallel education layer that complements schools and helps students move through a cycle of: evidence → direction → real project → feedback → new evidence What I learned Building Compass changed how I think about access. I began by asking: Who gets good guidance? Then I realized there was another question: Who gets to build? When more people can build, more problems can be solved by the people who understand them best. That is how progress compounds. Limitations The submitted judge path is local and synthetic; it is not a production-scale claim. It does not predict admissions outcomes or guarantee educational results. The offline preview does not exercise production persistence, delivery, or remote model calls. Only fictional data is used in the judge flow. What's next V5 is being rebuilt around family feedback, verified university information, admissions expertise, clearer reading hierarchy, and more specific activity and resource recommendations. The goal remains simple: help more students find a path that truly fits them.

title: KYT(Kiken Yochi Training) Lab — Education That Saves Lives
description: Japan cut workplace deaths ~90% with daily hazard training (KYT). KYT Lab brings it to the world: team sessions on AI-generated work scenes, coached by GPT-5.6. AI proposes, people decide.
about:
KYT Lab — Education That Saves Lives I hope KYT Lab helps protect someone, somewhere, from an injury or accident. Short Description Japan reduced workplace deaths by nearly 90%, supported by a participatory safety culture in which KYT is one important pillar. KYT Lab brings this practice to teams worldwide through collaborative sessions built around relevant workplace scenes and attempt-first coaching from GPT-5.6. AI proposes. People decide. Inspiration I am a chemist, not a software engineer. I hold a PhD in chemistry, have nine years of experience in the chemical industry, and have worked in laboratories and plants across Japan, Singapore, and the United States. The contrast among those workplaces taught me that safety is more than a set of written rules. It is a practiced habit of observation: what people notice, which weak signals they take seriously, and whether a team examines risk together before beginning work. The numbers show why this habit matters. The International Labour Organization estimates that nearly 3 million people die from work-related causes each year, while another 395 million suffer non-fatal injuries. Japan has demonstrated that sustained safety education and workplace practice can produce remarkable progress. Workplace deaths fell from 6,712 in 1961 to 746 in 2024—a reduction of nearly 90%. No single practice explains that achievement, but one pillar of Japan’s participatory safety culture is KYT: Kiken Yochi Training, or Hazard Prediction Training. Practiced in teams before work begins since 1974, KYT teaches people to examine a work scene, make hazards visible, compare perspectives, and agree on a practical action. KYT is one of the most valuable educational practices developed in Japanese workplaces, yet it has rarely crossed national borders. Language barriers, limited access to trained facilitators, and reliance on paper-based materials have kept much of the method local. Safety education is not only for schools. For the adults who build, manufacture, maintain, transport, and conduct research, it can be education that saves lives. I created KYT Lab to help this practice move beyond company walls and national borders. Who It Is For KYT Lab is designed for vocational educators, laboratory instructors, workplace safety trainers, supervisors, and team facilitators who want learners to practice hazard recognition together. It is particularly useful when generic safety materials do not resemble the learners’ actual work. An instructor can prepare a relevant scene, invite the team, facilitate the discussion, and preserve the resulting evidence and decisions as a learning record. What It Does KYT Lab transforms the traditional pen-and-paper KYT session into an authenticated, real-time collaborative web experience—without replacing the fundamentals of the method. A facilitator begins by describing the actual task. They can upload an existing workplace image or use gpt-image-2 to generate a relevant, text-free training scene. Before using a generated scene, the facilitator reviews it for suitability. Participants then join the same live session and move through the four rounds of KYT. Round 1 — Observe Learners study the image, place evidence markers directly on the scene, and explain the causal chain: condition → action → incident Each danger statement remains linked to a normalized image coordinate, ensuring that the evidence refers to the same location on every participant’s screen. GPT-5.6 KYT Coach The coach appears only after the learner has made an initial attempt. Its feedback follows a strengths-first structure: What the learner did well One focused area for improvement An editable example, when helpful Suggestions are never inserted silently. The learner decides whether to edit, use, or ignore them. Round 2 — Prioritize Participants compare their observations and vote on the most important danger. Voting supports the discussion, but it does not make the decision. The facilitator explicitly selects the team’s focus danger. Round 3 — Plan The team converts the selected danger into a practical, verifiable action: Who will act? What will they do? When will they do it? How will the team confirm that it was completed? Round 4 — Commit The session closes with one observable team goal and a shared Look–Point–Check–Call. The team points, confirms the action, and repeats its final CHECK! call together. Learning Record The final report connects: Visual evidence Danger statements Team votes Facilitator decisions Practical actions Participation AI coaching history The final team commitment This report is a formative learning record—not a compliance certificate or an automated declaration that a workplace is safe. Why This Is Different Most AI safety products try to identify hazards for the user. KYT Lab is designed around the opposite goal: helping people become better at identifying, explaining, and discussing hazards themselves. The image is not an answer key. GPT-5.6 does not select the team’s priority, approve a control, or certify that a workplace is safe. The technology creates relevant practice, supports real-time collaboration, and provides structured feedback. Learners and facilitators remain responsible for every decision. KYT Lab does not replace safety judgment. It trains it. Responsible AI Boundaries Safety training is a high-stakes use of AI, so I designed explicit limits into the product: Learners make their own attempt before receiving AI feedback. Coaching begins by recognizing what the learner did well. Suggestions are advisory, editable, and never applied silently. Facilitators make all prioritization and final decisions. Generated scenes must be reviewed before training. Structured Outputs constrain coaching to the intended educational format. OpenAI response storage is disabled by default. The human-led training process can continue if an AI request fails. KYT Lab does not replace hazard elimination, engineering controls, safe work procedures, task-specific risk assessments, competent supervision, legal requirements, or professional safety judgment. Teams must verify all AI-generated content before using it. AI proposes. People decide. How We Built It ChatGPT Pro helped me explain a Japanese educational method clearly in English. Codex with GPT-5.6 then became a hands-on engineering collaborator. I supplied the KYT domain knowledge, defined the educational workflow, and made every product and safety decision. Codex helped translate those decisions into working software. Together, we turned the four-round pedagogy into a TypeScript monorepo using: React 19 and Vite for the responsive web experience ElysiaJS on Bun for the API and session workflow Better Auth for authenticated facilitator and participant access PostgreSQL and Prisma for scenarios, evidence, decisions, coaching history, and reports Redis pub/sub and WebSockets for presence and real-time collaboration Local or S3-compatible storage for private images and durable image-generation jobs GPT-5.6 through the OpenAI Responses API for schema-constrained coaching Zod schemas and Structured Outputs to keep coaching within the intended educational format gpt-image-2 for relevant, text-free workplace scenes Playwright and Bun tests for unit, integration, security, authorization, collaboration, and end-to-end coverage Docker, Kubernetes, and Argo CD for production deployment The architecture is more than a model prompt: Browser → Elysia API → PostgreSQL
                    ├→ Redis pub/sub and WebSockets
                    ├→ Private image storage
                    └→ OpenAI text and image models Shared TypeScript types and validation rules connect the interface, API, database, and real-time events. This is essential because every evidence marker, danger statement, vote, decision, and report entry must remain synchronized and attributable. Challenges We Encountered Real-Time Group Work Collaboration is not an optional feature of KYT—it is the pedagogy. Learners must see what others noticed, compare interpretations, vote, and reach a shared decision. Collaboration therefore could not be implemented as a simple commenting feature. Markers, danger statements, votes, facilitator decisions, and team calls had to synchronize live over WebSockets while preserving identity, permissions, and authorship. Keeping AI Advisory It is easy to build an AI system that gives an answer. It is much harder to build one that waits, listens, and coaches. A system that immediately identifies every hazard might create an impressive demonstration, but it would remove the exact thinking that KYT is intended to develop. I therefore designed an attempt-first learning loop: the learner observes and explains first, and the coach responds afterward with strengths-first guidance. The goal was not to maximize how much the model could do. It was to decide where the model should stop. Preserving Evidence Precision A marker and its danger statement form a single learning object. If their coordinates, ownership, edits, or deletion become unsynchronized, the final learning record can become misleading. KYT Lab uses normalized image coordinates, shared validation rules, database persistence, and real-time events to keep evidence traceable across different screens and devices. Creating Relevant Scenes Generic illustrations often disengage learners because they do not resemble the work being discussed. Generated scenes therefore needed to be relevant, realistic, free of embedded text, and reviewed by the instructor before use. The image is a surface for discussion—not an automatically generated risk assessment. Authorization and Privacy A collaborative safety application can contain private team membership information, work descriptions, uploaded images, and learning records. The system therefore required server-derived identity, distinct facilitator and participant permissions, protected file access, private cache controls, secure session handling, and tests covering cross-team and cross-session access. Accomplishments and Lessons Learned I am most proud that I translated a participatory safety practice I knew from Japanese industry into an English-language collaborative learning experience without turning it into an autonomous safety tool. My professional background is in chemistry and workplace safety, not software engineering. During one Build Week, I created an authenticated, real-time application with relevant scenarios, structured coaching, explicit human decision gates, and durable learning reports. The accomplishment is not only that the application works. It is that the technology preserves the central principle of KYT: People learn by making their observations visible, comparing perspectives, and reaching a practical commitment together. The larger lesson is that AI can help domain experts turn valuable local practices into software that people around the world can use. As a non-native English speaker, I know how easily useful knowledge can remain confined by language and tooling. ChatGPT helped me express the method clearly, while Codex helped me implement it as a working product. That path—from domain expert to creator of a shipped educational tool—is the possibility I care about most. Validation and Intended Impact This submission demonstrates a working product and a repeatable training workflow. It is not a completed field-efficacy study. I reviewed the workflow, coaching boundaries, and generated content using my experience in chemistry and industrial workplaces. I also verified the software through unit, integration, security, authorization, collaboration, and Playwright end-to-end tests. What Can Be Verified Today A live deployment supporting the complete four-round method Seven ready-to-use worked scenarios Authenticated facilitator and participant roles Real-time collaborative markers, votes, and decisions Evidence linked to normalized image coordinates Attempt-first GPT-5.6 coaching Explicit human acceptance or rejection of AI suggestions Durable learning reports A public repository with automated test coverage and deployment documentation I am not claiming that this prototype has reduced workplace incidents. Demonstrating that outcome will require careful, long-term, real-world evidence. The next validation step is to conduct structured pilots with vocational instructors, laboratory educators, and workplace trainers. I want to measure whether repeated practice improves: The quality of observable evidence Cause-to-outcome reasoning The specificity of practical actions Participation and team communication The goal is to measure learning—not simply whether participants enjoyed using the application. What’s Next 1. Measure Learning Develop a before-and-after rubric for hazard observation, causal reasoning, action specificity, and team communication. 2. Pilot With Educators Work with vocational instructors, laboratory educators, and workplace trainers to evaluate KYT Lab in real facilitated sessions. 3. Cross the Language Barrier Fully Support multilingual sessions while preserving KYT’s Japanese concepts and facilitator-led character. 4. Support Instructors Add aggregate views that reveal common reasoning gaps without turning the product into an automated safety-scoring system. 5. Prepare for Responsible Organizational Use Strengthen data-retention controls, scenario-review workflows, facilitator guidance, and organizational privacy settings. The long-term goal is not to automate safety judgment. It is to make high-quality hazard-prediction practice more relevant, repeatable, and accessible. KYT is one proven local educational practice. I believe the same pattern—preserving domain expertise, reducing language barriers, and keeping human judgment central—can help other valuable methods cross borders as well. Try It Out Live application: https://kytlab.rxx.jp Three-minute demonstration: https://youtu.be/kGLp1Vifssc GitHub repository: https://github.com/Ameyanagi/KYTLab For the fastest review, watch the three-minute demonstration first. Then open the live application and follow one worked scenario from visual evidence to the final team commitment. To experience the real-time collaboration, invite a second participant and open the session in two separate browser profiles. I would especially value feedback from safety educators, vocational instructors, laboratory leaders, and workplace trainers who facilitate participatory learning. I hope KYT Lab helps protect someone, somewhere, from an injury or accident.

title: The Missing Chart
description: The Missing Chart: Learn how incomplete and evolving patient information changes AI-assisted clinical reasoning.
about: Inspiration As a doctor, I understand that clinical reasoning rarely begins with a complete picture. Patient information arrives over time, and clinicians constantly reconsider their thinking as new symptoms, medications, laboratory results, and outside records become available. Through my work across healthcare and AI, I have also seen a persistent divide. Many clinicians hesitate to trust AI because it can produce confident responses based on incomplete context or misunderstand clinical nuance. At the same time, AI engineers may understand the technology without fully understanding how medicine is practiced or how clinical decisions evolve. I built The Missing Chart to help bridge that gap. It reflects how I think as a clinician: reason with what is currently known, recognize what is missing, verify consequential claims, and revise the assessment when the evidence changes. What it does The Missing Chart is an interactive clinical education simulation built around an evolving synthetic patient record. Learners review the information available at a specific point in care, decide what to include in a focused request, examine the resulting assessment, and identify claims that require verification. As new records become available, they reassess the patient and see how missing context can change the interpretation, urgency, and appropriate next steps. Rather than treating AI output as a final answer, the simulation teaches learners to examine the relationship between the information supplied and the response received. How we built it I designed the clinical scenario, educational objectives, evolving-information structure, and verification activities using my background in medicine, health informatics, and healthcare AI evaluation. I used Codex to translate that clinical concept into a working application, including the interface, timeline progression, record-selection logic, deterministic response pathways, accessibility improvements, testing, and repository refinement. GPT-5.6 supported clinical-language refinement, safety review, debugging, and evaluation of the learner workflow. The application was built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Node.js and deployed through OpenAI Sites. Its deterministic structure gives every learner a consistent experience without requiring an API key or credits. Challenges we ran into The central challenge was representing how clinical information evolves without making the experience confusing. The application needed to distinguish between information that exists somewhere in the patient’s record and information that is actually available to the clinician at that moment. Another challenge was making the generated assessment useful without allowing it to appear complete or authoritative. The experience had to show that an output may be internally reasonable and still be clinically insufficient because important context was never included. I also had to translate clinical reasoning into explicit application logic. Clinicians often integrate uncertainty, missing evidence, and changing priorities intuitively. Turning that process into a structured and understandable simulation required careful design. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am proud that The Missing Chart represents a recognizable clinical problem rather than a simplified question-and-answer exercise. Information selection directly affects the assessment shown to the learner. The simulation makes missing context visible and allows learners to compare an initially reasonable response with a revised assessment after new evidence appears. The application also brings clinical education, AI literacy, safety, and evaluation into one workflow. It uses entirely synthetic patient information, requires no login or credentials, and keeps interpretation and responsibility with the human learner. What we learned Building The Missing Chart reinforced that safe clinical AI use is not only about whether an answer is correct. It is also about whether the model received the right information, whether important evidence is absent, and whether the user knows which claims require verification. I also learned that clinicians and AI developers often describe the same problem differently. Clinicians think in terms of evolving evidence, uncertainty, and consequences. Developers often think in terms of inputs, outputs, and system behavior. Effective clinical AI tools must connect both perspectives. The project also showed that a single interactive workflow can serve several purposes: clinical education, AI-literacy training, evaluation of human-AI interaction, and structured testing of how systems respond to incomplete information. What's next for The Missing Chart The next version could include cases from multiple specialties, different patterns of missing information, configurable timelines, and more detailed feedback for learners. An AI-powered backend could also help educators generate and validate synthetic clinical scenarios, create controlled variations in the information available at each stage, and test how different models respond as the chart evolves. With appropriate clinical review and privacy safeguards, these interactions could produce structured evaluation data for future AI training and safety research. The long-term goal is broader than one simulation. The Missing Chart could become a shared environment where clinicians learn how to work with AI, developers learn how clinical reasoning actually unfolds, and researchers generate better evidence for building safer medical AI systems. Multiple problems, one connected solution.

title: Vocaby.app features the "Adaptive Story Coach"
description: An accessible AI story coach that turns each learner’s own vocabulary into personalized stories, contextual practice, listening exercises, and pronunciation feedback.
about: Inspiration Vocabulary apps often teach words in isolation. Learners may collect hundreds of useful words, but still struggle to understand and use them in a meaningful context. Vocaby's Adaptive Story Coach turns the words a learner actually needs into a small, accessible learning journey: understand them in a coherent story, hear them, inspect their grammar, practise them, and make the result count toward progress. What it does The Story Coach selects six words from the signed-in learner's vocabulary. Learners can optionally choose up to three wish words, while Vocaby fills the remaining places with words that are new, due, or have caused difficulty. GPT-5.6 creates a short coherent story, a faithful translation, and contextual explanations. The result becomes a complete learning loop: Listen to the story with synchronized reading support Reveal inline translations Open target words for translation, context, and audio Inspect sentence grammar and individual prepositions Complete a supported cloze exercise Solve a sentence-order puzzle Practise pronunciation sentence by sentence Save up to five stories in a personal Story Book Feed exercise results back into the learner's existing progress How we built it Vocaby uses a Vue 3 and Capacitor frontend for web, iOS, and Android, with a NestJS and MongoDB backend. The Story Coach uses the OpenAI Responses API with GPT-5.6 and a strict structured-output schema. The server selects vocabulary from real learner state, validates every generated response, confirms that the target words are present, and rejects malformed or linguistically invalid output before it reaches the learner. OpenAI text-to-speech provides natural story and sentence audio. Deterministic application code handles navigation, validation, scoring, storage, and progress updates rather than asking the model to control the learning state. Accessibility Accessibility shaped the feature throughout development. The experience includes semantic focus management, stable screen-reader announcements, content-language metadata, reduced-motion support, scalable mobile layouts, and 44-pixel touch targets. Story audio is deliberately delayed so it does not overlap VoiceOver announcements. We tested the experience with automated axe regressions, responsive browser measurements, native iOS and Android builds, and physical VoiceOver and TalkBack checks. Challenges we faced One challenge was balancing learner choice with genuine adaptation. Allowing unlimited chosen words would make the feature less responsive to learning state, so we limited wish words to three and let the coach select the remaining vocabulary. Generated language also required deterministic validation. During a real Italian generation test, we detected the incorrect construction “su il calcio.” We converted that discovery into a validator and prompt regression before accepting the next result. Mobile accessibility presented another challenge. Screen-reader announcements initially overlapped story audio, focus could return to outdated interface elements, and iOS microphone permission had to be requested directly from a user action. Testing on physical devices helped us resolve behavior that automated tests alone could not reveal. What we learned Generative content only becomes a learning product when it leads to an understandable next action and measurable progress. We also learned that AI generation works best inside deterministic boundaries: GPT-5.6 creates the linguistic material, while application code validates the result and controls the learner's data. Finally, accessibility cannot be treated as a final checklist. Testing it throughout development improved the product for every learner. What existed before Build Week Vocaby existed before OpenAI Build Week with authentication, vocabulary storage, live translation, learning counters, and existing training tools. During the July 13–21 submission period, we built the complete Adaptive Story Coach vertical slice with Codex: adaptive word selection, wish-word mixing, GPT-5.6 generation and validation, contextual story audio, Story Book, practice exercises, grammar reuse, native integration, and accessibility hardening. Codex helped analyze the existing architecture, implement across Vue and NestJS, create regression tests, diagnose real-device behavior, and maintain a living feature specification. The core product decisions remained human-led. What's next The next step is bounded pronunciation assessment using speech recognition, without replacing the accessible and ungraded pronunciation practice. We also want to expand the accessibility work from the Story Coach into the rest of Vocaby.
